metaDescription: Five push lawn sweepers from 21 to 30 inches that list for under $300, ranked on drive design, hopper volume, frame stiffness and long-term upkeep.
expertTake: The VEVOR 30 inch with the 12 cubic foot hopper is the best pick for big open lawns where you refuse to buy a tractor attachment. The Scotts 26 inch is the value pick for owners who want a known name and a simple layout. Skip the whole tier if your property is mostly slopes, because a wide push sweeper is hard work uphill.
introParagraphs: At the top of the budget range, the changes that matter are drive design and hopper size rather than extra brushes. A push sweeper is still wheel powered, so better wheels, a stiffer frame and a drive that does not lock up on a sharp turn are what you are really paying for.

The honest ceiling is the human pushing it. Width and volume can grow, but the machine does not get any easier to move. This guide ranks the options by how well their size suits the effort involved, and by what is likely to wear out first. Prices move, and the $300 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: VEVOR 30 in push sweeper, 12 cu ft hopper, V brushes
products.description:
At 30 inches wide and 12 cubic feet of hopper, this is the largest push sweeper in the lineup. Wider machines cover a lawn in fewer lanes, and the big bag means you can finish several lanes before walking to the pile. The brush set is three V-shaped brushes, a design that angles the bristles inward so debris is guided toward the middle of the path instead of spilling off the sides. It also lists a 1:5 ratio between brush and wheel, which is the drive figure that decides how hard the brushes throw leaves into the bag. Ten numbered height levels give you repeatable settings, so you can mark a number for lawn and another for driveway and return to them.

The cost of the size is storage and effort. A 30 inch machine will not fit through many garden gates, and a full 12 cubic foot bag of wet clippings is heavy enough to make you stop. Next to the Scotts 26 inch in this list, you gain about four inches of path and a much bigger bag, but you give up the lighter handling and the easier garage fit.

Ownership is bag care and bolts. Dry the fabric after each use, rinse caked clippings off the V brushes, and check the axle hardware at season start. If your lawn is open and flat, this model is the one that finishes fastest, and the numbered height dial keeps the setup fast between sessions.
products.bestFor: Large open lawns where a wide path and big bag save the most time.
pros: Thirty inch path cuts total lanes
Twelve cubic foot bag lengthens each run
Ten numbered height levels repeat well
V brushes funnel debris to the centre
cons: Will not pass through narrow gates
Full bag is heavy to push and lift

products.name: Scotts LSW70026S 26 in push lawn sweeper
products.description:
Scotts sells this sweeper under a familiar lawn-care name, and the listing guidance is practical. It tells you the correct brush height is essential and that the brushes should only lightly contact the top of the grass. Set too high, they miss clippings, and set too low, they drag and wear.

The 26 inch width is the middle of the push-sweeper range, so it is wide enough to be efficient but narrow enough for most garden gates. The listing frames it as best for light coverage on level lawns, so it is not marketed as a heavy-duty machine, and that restraint is useful when you compare it with 12 cubic foot units that overpromise. Set beside the Earthwise 21 inch, the Scotts covers about a quarter more ground each pass. Measured against the VEVOR 30 inch, it is lighter and easier to store but takes more passes.

Expect the fabric bag to be the first part to need replacing, usually after a few seasons of sun exposure. Keep the brushes clear of wrapped grass, tighten the wheel hardware and dry the bag before folding it away.
products.bestFor: Level suburban lawns that want a mid-width, recognisable brand.
pros: Clear guidance on brush height setup
Mid width fits most garden gates
cons: Light-duty design struggles with heavy leaf drifts
Limited detail on bag volume in the listing

products.name: GreenSweep Pickup Pro V26 push sweeper, AntiLock Drive
products.description:
The GreenSweep stands out for its drive system. Most push sweepers lock the brush shaft to the wheel, so when you stop pushing on a slope, or turn sharply, the brushes can bind and the machine fights you. An anti-lock style drive uncouples the brush from the wheel in a way that lets you pivot without the shaft stalling.

That mechanical detail matters most in tight garden layouts, where you turn every few metres. The listing also highlights fast brush rotation for leaves, clippings and light garden debris, and a fully manual design with no cables or batteries. Compared with the Scotts 26 inch, the GreenSweep adds that specialised drive, though it carries a less established brand history. Against the VEVOR 30, it takes more lanes but turns more easily.

In year three you should check the drive clutch for debris, because anything that wraps the shaft will defeat the anti-lock action. Keep it clean, store the bag dry and look at the wheel bearings annually.
products.bestFor: Gardens with many turns where a locking drive would fight you.
pros: Fast brush spin lifts leaves cleanly
No cables, fuel or battery to manage
cons: Newer brand with less service history
Extra drive parts add a maintenance point

products.name: Splendor LS-650A2 26 in walk-behind sweeper
products.description:
This unit markets itself as both a lawn sweeper and a road sweeper, which makes it the pick for properties with a gravel apron, a long driveway or a sidewalk strip. The listing stresses a rugged build and a simple assembly, which suggests a basic frame and fewer fiddly parts.

The brush height adjusts to the grass, so the same machine can be lowered for pavement. Pavement is rougher on bristles than turf, so plan on earlier tuft wear than you would see on grass alone. It shares the 26 inch path with the Scotts and GreenSweep, but the listing gives little on bag volume, so confirm fit before ordering spares. Compared with the Earthwise 21 inch, it sweeps a wider strip per pass.

Upkeep is brush rinsing, dry bag storage and an occasional bolt check. If you sweep gritty surfaces, flush the shaft ends now and then so the bearings do not grind.
products.bestFor: Properties with driveway, gravel or sidewalk edges beside the lawn.
pros: Built for lawn and road sweeping

products.name: Earthwise LSW70021 21 in leaf and grass sweeper
products.description:
The Earthwise is the small-footprint option, and it is open about its limits. It is meant for dry leaves and light debris on short, recently mowed, relatively level lawns, and it says tall grass and uneven ground are poor matches. That makes buying decisions easier than with units that claim to do everything.

Its four brushes split into two sections, so each pair follows the ground separately. For a small lot with beds and a patio, a 21 inch machine is much easier to turn than any 26 or 30 inch rival. Next to the VEVOR 30 inch, it covers far less area per pass, which is its limit on larger lawns. It is the right size for a courtyard or townhouse yard.

It has been on the market a long time, so spares and instructions are easy to find. Clean the brushes, dry the bag and store it where the bristles do not rest on the floor.
products.bestFor: Small, flat yards that need a nimble sweeper.
cons: Narrow path means many passes on big lawns
Poor on tall, wet or rough turf

buyingCriteria.explanation: A standard push sweeper couples the brush shaft directly to the wheels, so a sharp turn can make the brushes drag. The GreenSweep's anti-lock drive is built to avoid that. If your yard has many turns, a design that lets the brush freewheel is worth more than a bigger bag. If your yard is a straight open lawn, a locked drive works fine. Ask yourself how many times per lap you reverse or pivot: more than a handful, and the freewheeling design earns its keep. Also check whether the drive is a sealed unit or exposed, since an exposed clutch collects leaf debris and needs more frequent cleaning.

The VEVOR 30 inch covers a lot of ground, but its overall width is wider than the path and many garden gates are 36 inches. Measure your narrowest opening before you buy. A 26 inch frame like the Scotts or Splendor is the common compromise. Remember to allow room for the handle and the bag when you turn at a fence line, since the bag sticks out behind the brush and catches on posts. A tape measure at the gate takes thirty seconds and saves a return.

The VEVOR 30's 12 cubic feet is the largest bag in the list, and it is also the one most likely to be too heavy to lift when full of damp debris. Consider emptying it halfway on wet days. Small bags like the Earthwise's are easier to handle but fill fast. A practical rule is to size the bag to the distance from the lawn to your dump spot: the farther you carry, the more a larger bag saves. Emptying into a tarp rather than a bin also lets you drag the load instead of lifting it.

Ten numbered levels on the VEVOR 30 let two people use the same setting. Stepless knobs are finer but harder to repeat. Scotts stresses that the brushes should lightly touch the top of the grass, so choose a system you can set quickly. Test it by doing a short strip, looking at what is left behind, and adjusting one level at a time. Do this each time you switch from damp morning grass to afternoon dry grass, because the ideal height drifts with the thickness of the turf.

Pavement and gravel wear bristles faster than turf. The Splendor markets itself for lawn and road, so it expects that wear. Others are lawn-first, and sweeping a driveway with them shortens brush life.

Push effort rises quickly with width and bag weight on a slope. A 30 inch sweeper with a full hopper is a serious pull uphill. Level yards suit every unit here, while hilly yards suit narrow units like the Earthwise. On a slope, sweep across rather than straight up and down, and empty the bag before it is full, because a heavy hopper makes the machine want to roll back on you. Anything steeper than a gentle grade is better handled with a blower.

specDecoder.meaning: How many times the brush turns per wheel revolution. A higher ratio gives faster brush speed at walking pace.
specDecoder.watchFor: The VEVOR 30 states 1:5; the others in this list do not print a figure.

specDecoder.meaning: V-shaped brushes angle bristles to guide debris toward the middle. Straight brushes throw it straight back.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the VEVOR 30 lists V-shaped brushes here.

specDecoder.meaning: Bag capacity in cubic feet, which sets how far you sweep between dumps.
specDecoder.watchFor: The VEVOR 30 holds 12, while the Scotts, Splendor and GreenSweep listings are less specific.

specDecoder.meaning: How the wheel power reaches the brush. An anti-lock design lets the brush freewheel on turns.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GreenSweep is the only one advertising AntiLock Drive.

specDecoder.meaning: The lawn or pavement conditions the maker designs for.
specDecoder.watchFor: Scotts and Earthwise both say level, mowed turf, and Splendor adds road use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drive and brush layout
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how each sweeper gets wheel power to the brushes. The GreenSweep's anti-lock drive and the VEVOR 30's 1:5 ratio earned credit. Listings with no drive detail scored lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Width, bag volume and expected weight were weighed together. The 30 inch VEVOR gains on speed but loses on gate fit. The 21 inch Earthwise gains on handling.

howWeEvaluated.title: Frame and parts
howWeEvaluated.description: Frame build and spare availability came from the listings. Established names like Scotts and Earthwise scored for parts. Newer brands scored on stated design features.

howWeEvaluated.title: Honesty of limits
howWeEvaluated.description: Listings that stated clear conditions earned trust. Scotts and Earthwise both name level, mowed lawns as their domain. Claims of percentage pickup were ignored.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cap compliance
howWeEvaluated.description: Every pick was checked against the $300 cap at the time of writing. Items with no current listing at or below the cap were removed. This guide shares no more than two products with its lower-cap sibling.

cards.label: 30 inch (VEVOR)
cards.text: Fewer lanes and a 12 cubic foot bag, but it needs wide gates and a strong back.

cards.label: 26 inch (Scotts, GreenSweep, Splendor)
cards.text: Easier storage and turning, with a modest loss in speed on open lawn.

howToChoose.note: Choose the VEVOR for open ground and a 26 inch unit for anything with gates or beds.

howToChoose.subheading: For Driveway and Lawn Together Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A brush that adjusts down to hard surfaces and a rugged frame. Pavement grit wears bristles and bearings quickly, so replaceable tufts matter.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Splendor LS-650A2 is the clearest fit. The VEVOR 30 can do it too with its ten levels, but it is wider than most driveways need.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your lawn is over half an acre, hilly or leafy. A tow-behind sweeper pulled by a tractor outperforms any push unit in this list.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your lot is small and level. The Earthwise or Scotts covers it with far less effort.

maintenance.task: Dry and shake out the bag
maintenance.why: Damp fabric mildews and weakens. A big bag takes longer to dry.
Wrapped grass binds the shaft. On the GreenSweep it also stops the anti-lock action.
Vibration loosens bolts. A loose wheel slips and the brushes stall.
Worn bristle tips stop reaching the grass. Pavement sweeping speeds the wear.
Sand and dust grind bearings. A short rinse extends their life.

faq.q: Is a 30 inch sweeper too big for a home lawn?
faq.a: It depends on your gates and your back. On an open lawn it saves many lanes. On a lot with narrow gates or slopes, a 26 inch unit is more practical.

faq.q: What does the top of the cap buy over cheaper sweepers?
faq.a: Width, a much larger bag and, in a few cases, a better drive design. It does not buy a motor, so effort still depends on you.

faq.q: How do I set the brush height?
faq.a: Lower the brushes until the tips just touch the top of the grass blades. Too high leaves clippings and too low drags and wears the bristles.

faq.q: Can I sweep a driveway with a lawn sweeper?
faq.a: Yes, on loose dry debris, though pavement wears the bristles faster. The Splendor is the one marketed for it.

faq.q: Will it pick up wet leaves?
faq.a: Not well. Wet leaves clog the brush and fill the bag with dead weight. Use a blower for those.

Listing prices move over time. The cap reflects prices when this guide was updated, so check the live listing. If a pick has crept above the cap since then, the next model down in this list is the sensible swap.
